title: Air Jordan
hook: A deal meant to sell $3m of shoes built a brand worth billions a year.
situation: In 1984 Nike was behind in basketball, and Michael Jordan was a rookie who preferred Adidas. Nike bet heavily on one young player instead of spreading its money across many.
exchange: Nike paid Jordan and gave him his own shoe line. Jordan gave Nike his name, his game and, over time, an entire brand.
brought: Money, design and a signature shoe built around one player.
Talent, fame and, eventually, a brand bigger than the shoe.
turning_point: The Air Jordan 1 went on sale in 1985. Nike had reportedly hoped for $3m of sales in its first years, and it sold about $126m in the first year.
measure: First-year Air Jordan sales against Nike’s reported target of $3m. By fiscal 2022 Nike’s finance chief put the Jordan Brand at about $5bn
evidence: The first-year figure is widely repeated but rarely sourced, and the original terms were never disclosed. The later revenue comes from Nike itself. Together they show a partnership that grew far beyond what either side signed.
lesson: The best deals give the partner a stake in the upside, not just a fee. Jordan earned from the brand he helped build.
take: The deal every athlete negotiation is compared to. The price was ordinary. The structure, a brand around one person, was not.

creative.label: Watch ‘A People’s History of the Air Jordan 1’ on Jordan’s channel

announcement: Read the deal’s history · Fox Business
links: See the endorsement record · Guinness World Records
deal_value: Never disclosed. Guinness World Records lists it at $2.5m

title: Three Films, Then Everything
data_source: Pixar’s films, Disney’s money and reach
hook: A three-film deal ended with Disney buying its partner for $7.4bn.
situation: Pixar was a small computer animation company. Disney had the money, marketing and cinemas to release films around the world.
exchange: In 1991 Disney agreed to finance and distribute three Pixar films. Pixar would deliver the finished films.
brought: Computer animation and storytelling no studio could match.
turning_point: The deal produced Toy Story in 1995, the first fully computer-animated feature film. After disputes, including over whether Toy Story 2 counted, Disney bought Pixar in 2006.
measure: The value Disney put on Pixar fifteen years after the first deal. Steve Jobs became Disney’s largest shareholder
evidence: The 2006 price shows what the partnership had built: Disney paid billions for the partner it had once financed. The films’ box office belongs to both sides, and no source splits the gains.
lesson: When a partner becomes the source of your best work, the partnership will end in a purchase or a parting. Plan for both.
take: The most expensive way to end a partnership is to buy your partner. Disney decided it was cheaper than losing them.
deal_value: 1991 terms not disclosed. 2006 acquisition worth about $7.4bn in Disney shares

title: The Emirates Stadium
hook: An airline put its name on a new stadium before it opened.
situation: Arsenal was building a new 60,000-seat stadium and needed money to pay for it. Emirates wanted a global brand in London.
exchange: Emirates paid for the stadium’s name and the front of Arsenal’s shirts. Arsenal got long-term money while it paid for the stadium.
brought: About £100m for naming rights and shirt sponsorship.
A new stadium, a global fan base and the shirt.
turning_point: Signed in October 2004, the deal covered the stadium’s name for 15 years and the shirt for eight. The stadium opened in 2006.
measure: The reported value of the naming and shirt deal. A deal term, not a result
evidence: No result has been published for either side. The best evidence is behaviour: Emirates renewed in 2012 for £150m, extended the naming rights to 2028, and Arsenal’s own films have announced further extensions since.
lesson: If you can’t see the results, watch the renewals. A sponsor that keeps paying more has found something worth it.
take: The renewals tell you more than the original price. Twenty years on, both sides keep choosing each other.
deal_value: About £100m in 2004, then £150m in a 2012 renewal

title: The Deal Mastercard Lost
hook: FIFA swapped its payments partner, and ended up in court.
situation: Mastercard had sponsored the World Cup for years and expected to renew. FIFA negotiated with Visa at the same time.
exchange: Visa agreed an eight-year sponsorship from 2007. FIFA got a bigger fee, and Visa got the world’s most watched tournament.
brought: $180m over eight years, according to its own filing.
Exclusive payments rights to the World Cup.
turning_point: In December 2006 a New York court ruled that FIFA had breached its agreement with Mastercard. FIFA settled with Mastercard, and Visa became the sponsor.
metric_label: Visa’s payments over eight years, per its SEC filing
measure: The total contractual payments disclosed in Visa’s filings. A deal term, not a result
evidence: Visa’s own filing confirms the price, which is rare. Neither side published a return, and the settlement figure comes from a single secondary source.
lesson: An exclusive partnership is only as good as your partner’s other promises. Check what they have already agreed with others.
take: The most reliable price in this edition came out because of a lawsuit and a share listing, not because anyone chose to share it.
deal_value: $180m over eight years, disclosed in Visa’s SEC filings. Mastercard’s settlement was reported at about $90m

title: The Record Shirt
hook: A car brand paid a record sum for a football shirt.
situation: Manchester United was preparing to list its shares and wanted to show sponsorship growth. General Motors wanted Chevrolet to be a global brand.
exchange: Chevrolet became United’s shirt sponsor from 2014, paying roughly twice what the previous sponsor, Aon, had paid.
brought: Record shirt money and a global marketing push.
One of the most watched shirts in world sport.
turning_point: Signed in July 2012, the deal began with smaller payments of about $18.6m a season before Chevrolet’s name went on the shirt in 2014.
metric_label: Total payable to 2021, per United’s SEC filing
measure: The total disclosed in Manchester United’s filing, starting at $70m a season and rising 2.1% a year
evidence: The price is unusually well documented because United was listing on the New York Stock Exchange. No figure shows what Chevrolet gained, and reports near the end suggested neither side wanted to renew.
lesson: A record price makes headlines on the day you sign. Decide what you will measure for the seven years after.
take: United needed the number for investors. Chevrolet bought the most visible shirt in football. Only one of them published what they got.
deal_value: About $559m through 2020/21, disclosed in Manchester United’s SEC filing

title: The Player Nike Passed On
hook: Nike didn’t match the offer. Curry became the most influential player of his era.
situation: In 2013 Stephen Curry was a promising but injury-prone player. Under Armour wanted a basketball star to compete with Nike.
exchange: Under Armour offered close to $4m a year, reportedly more than Nike’s offer, and built a shoe line around him.
brought: A bigger offer and a signature shoe.
A style of play that changed basketball, and a growing fan base.
turning_point: The Curry One launched in 2015 as Curry became the league’s most valuable player. A Curry Brand followed in 2020.
metric_label: Reported yearly value of the 2013 deal
measure: The reported annual value when Curry signed. A deal term, not a result
evidence: Curry’s shoes boosted Under Armour’s basketball sales in 2015 and 2016, according to analysts at the time, but the company never published what he added overall. The partnership was reported to have ended in late 2025.
lesson: The cheapest moment to sign a partner is before everyone else sees what they will become.
take: Under Armour bought the future at today’s price. Few brands are brave enough to do that.
announcement: Read about the signing · Business Insider
deal_value: Reported at close to $4m a year in 2013. Later extensions were not disclosed

title: For Life
hook: A deal for life, with a number nobody confirmed.
situation: Cristiano Ronaldo was among the most followed people on social media, and Nike had sponsored him since he was a teenager.
exchange: Nike extended its deal with Ronaldo for the rest of his life. Ronaldo would wear and promote Nike after his playing career.
brought: One of the biggest audiences of any person in the world.
turning_point: In November 2016 Nike announced the extension. Ronaldo said in a video that it was for life.
metric_label: Reported value, never confirmed by Nike
measure: A figure based on a press comparison with LeBron James’s lifetime deal. Nike disclosed no terms
evidence: The value is a media estimate. Nike announced the deal without its length or price, and published no result.
lesson: A lifetime deal bets on a partner’s fame outlasting their career. Ask what the partner will be worth when they stop playing.
take: Like Heineken’s Bond deal in Edition 01, the famous number is a guess. It’s still the number everyone remembers.
impact_source: Read the reported value · NBC Sports

title: Forty Shades
hook: A singer and a luxury group built a beauty brand together.
situation: Beauty brands offered few foundation shades for darker skin. Rihanna wanted to build a brand, and LVMH’s Kendo division developed beauty brands with founders.
exchange: LVMH’s Kendo brought product development, production and distribution through Sephora. Rihanna brought the vision, the name and her audience.
brought: The idea, the brand and an audience of millions.
turning_point: Fenty Beauty launched in September 2017 with 40 shades of foundation, and much of the range sold out.
metric_label: Sales by the end of 2018, per LVMH’s chairman
measure: Sales described by Bernard Arnault for the brand’s first full year and a bit. Forbes put 15-month revenue at $570m
evidence: The early sales figures come from LVMH’s chairman and Forbes. A widely repeated $72m first-month figure appears to measure media value, not sales.
lesson: When a partner brings an audience that a big company can’t reach, give them real ownership, not a licensing fee.
take: A celebrity brand that started from a real gap in the market. The partnership worked because the product would have been worth buying without the name.
impact_source: Read about the brand’s growth · Black Enterprise
deal_value: Reported at $10m for the 2016 agreement, unconfirmed

title: The Global Coffee Alliance
hook: Nestlé paid $7.15bn for the right to sell Starbucks coffee in shops.
situation: Starbucks sold coffee in its cafés but was less strong in supermarkets. Nestlé was the world’s biggest food company and wanted a premium coffee brand.
exchange: Nestlé paid for a perpetual global licence to sell Starbucks packaged coffee and tea. Starbucks kept buying and roasting the beans and managing the brand.
brought: $7.15bn up front and global grocery distribution.
Its brand, coffee and a $2bn packaged business.
turning_point: Agreed in May 2018, the alliance put Starbucks coffee on supermarket shelves and in capsules around the world.
metric_label: Incremental sales from new products, as reported by Nestlé
measure: New-product sales Nestlé reported in the alliance’s first year, on top of the business it took over
evidence: Nestlé reported early incremental sales. Starbucks used most of the proceeds for share buybacks. Neither side published a full return on the price.
lesson: A licence can turn a brand into cash today. Agree who controls the brand once someone else is selling it.
take: Starbucks sold the right to be in your kitchen and kept control of what’s in the cup. A clean split of what each side does best.
impact_source: Read about the early results · Fox Business
deal_value: $7.15bn paid up front for a perpetual licence

title: Compute for Models
data_source: Microsoft’s money and cloud, OpenAI’s models
hook: A tech giant invested in a research lab, and the lab built ChatGPT.
situation: OpenAI needed vast computing power to train its models. Microsoft wanted a lead in artificial intelligence for its cloud and its products.
exchange: Microsoft invested money and became OpenAI’s exclusive cloud provider. OpenAI trained its models on Microsoft’s Azure.
brought: Investment and the Azure cloud to train models on.
Research and models Microsoft could build into its products.
turning_point: Microsoft invested $1bn in 2019 and more in 2021. After ChatGPT’s launch in late 2022, it announced a multiyear, multibillion-dollar investment in January 2023.
measure: The first investment. The 2023 amount was not disclosed and was reported at $10bn
evidence: The partnership changed the technology industry, but neither company has published what it added to Microsoft’s revenue. Its terms have also changed several times since.
lesson: When you invest in a partner’s capability, agree in advance how much independence they keep as they grow.
take: The partnership that set off the AI race. The money is famous, the return is still being argued over, and the terms keep moving.
impact_source: Read the reported value · Bloomberg via Yahoo
deal_value: $1bn in 2019. The 2023 investment was reported at $10bn, not disclosed

title: The Exclusive
hook: Spotify paid to own the world’s biggest podcast, then let it go elsewhere.
situation: Spotify wanted podcasts to bring people to its app and keep them there. The Joe Rogan Experience was the most popular podcast in the world.
exchange: Spotify paid for exclusive rights to the show. Rogan got a huge guaranteed fee.
brought: A guaranteed fee and its global audience.
The biggest podcast audience in the world.
turning_point: The show moved exclusively to Spotify in 2020. In 2024 a new deal ended the exclusivity, and the show returned to YouTube and Apple Podcasts.
measure: The widely reported value. The New York Times later reported it as more than $200m
evidence: Both values are press reports. Spotify didn’t publish what the exclusive added to subscribers or advertising, and its move away from exclusivity suggests the model didn’t pay as hoped.
lesson: Exclusivity buys control and costs reach. Decide which you need more before you pay for it.
take: Spotify paid to lock the door, then opened it again. The second deal tells you what the first one taught them.
impact_source: Read about the end of exclusivity · Star Tribune
deal_value: Reported at over $100m in 2020, and up to $250m for the 2024 non-exclusive deal. Spotify did not confirm either

title: Spotify Camp Nou
data_source: Spotify’s money, Barça’s stadium and shirt
hook: A cash-strapped club sold its stadium’s name for the first time.
situation: Barcelona was in deep financial trouble. Spotify, founded in Sweden, wanted a global stage beyond music.
exchange: Spotify took the front of the shirts and, for the first time, the stadium’s name. Barcelona got money it badly needed.
brought: Its shirts and one of the most famous stadiums in the world.
turning_point: From July 2022 the stadium became Spotify Camp Nou, the first name sold since it opened in 1957, and Spotify replaced Rakuten on the shirt.
measure: The figure first reported by a Catalan radio station. Neither side disclosed the terms or the exact length
evidence: The value is a press report, and reports even differ on how many years the deal runs. No result has been published for Spotify.
lesson: A partner in financial trouble may sell you something it never would have before. Make sure the value lasts after their trouble ends.
take: Spotify bought a name that had never been for sale. That scarcity was the real asset.
impact_source: Read the reported value · The Local

title: Oracle Red Bull Racing
data_source: Oracle’s money and cloud, Red Bull’s team
hook: A business software company put its name on a Formula 1 team.
situation: Honda was leaving Formula 1 and Red Bull Racing needed a new title partner. Oracle wanted to show its cloud to a global audience.
exchange: Oracle took the title of the team and supplied cloud computing for race strategy. Red Bull got money and data tools.
brought: Title sponsorship money and cloud computing for strategy.
A front-running team watched around the world.
turning_point: The team became Oracle Red Bull Racing at the launch of its 2022 car. Red Bull won the constructors’ championship that year and the next.
measure: A figure from an anonymous source quoted by the Associated Press. Neither side disclosed the terms
evidence: The value comes from one anonymous source. The team’s success is a fact, but no source shows what the sponsorship did for Oracle’s cloud business.
lesson: Sponsoring a winner is easy to celebrate and hard to measure. Decide in advance what a win should do for your business.
take: Oracle bought a seat next to the fastest car on the grid. Being a business brand, its real audience was the boardroom, not the grandstand.

creative.label: Watch ‘Introducing the RB18’ on Oracle’s channel

deal_value: Reported at about $100m a year for five years, from an anonymous source

title: Thursday Night Football
data_source: Amazon’s money and Prime, the NFL’s games
hook: Amazon paid about $1bn a year for one night of football a week.
situation: The NFL was the most watched sport in the US, mostly on traditional television. Amazon wanted more people to join and stay with Prime.
exchange: Amazon paid for the exclusive rights to Thursday Night Football, streamed on Prime Video. The NFL got a large fee and a younger, streaming audience.
brought: About $1bn a year and Prime Video’s reach.
Weekly games the US watches like nothing else.
turning_point: The first exclusive game, in September 2022, drew an average of about 13 million viewers by Nielsen’s count, and Amazon said it brought in a record number of Prime sign-ups.
metric_label: Prime sign-ups in a three-hour window, per Amazon
measure: Amazon’s internal memo said the first game beat Prime Day and Black Friday for sign-ups. It gave no total
evidence: The sign-up record comes from an Amazon memo with no number attached. Nielsen measured about 13 million viewers. Amazon has not published whether the deal pays back.
lesson: Buy content for the behaviour it drives in your core business, then measure that behaviour, not just the viewers.
take: Amazon didn’t buy football to sell football. It bought it to sell Prime, and judged it the same way.

creative.label: Watch ‘Football is Open’ on Prime Video’s channel

deal_value: Reported at about $1bn a year over 11 years

title: The $20bn Default
hook: Google pays Apple to be the search box on the iPhone.
situation: Most people never change the search engine their phone came with. For years Google has paid Apple to be the default in Safari, and the terms were secret.
exchange: Google pays Apple a share of the search advertising revenue it earns from Safari. Apple makes Google the default.
brought: Billions of dollars a year and the search engine people use.
The default position on hundreds of millions of iPhones.
turning_point: Documents in the US government’s antitrust case against Google showed it paid Apple $20bn in 2022, and testimony revealed the share as 36%.
metric_label: Google’s payment to Apple in 2022, per court documents
measure: The payment revealed in court. A witness disclosed that Apple receives 36% of Google’s search revenue from Safari
evidence: The figures are confirmed, but only because of an antitrust trial. They show what Google pays, not what being the default earns it, and the court’s concern was precisely that the deal shuts out rivals.
lesson: Paying to be the default can be worth more than any advertising, until a regulator decides it is too effective.
take: The biggest partnership payment in this archive is a default setting. It shows what distribution is worth, and what it can cost when regulators take notice.
announcement: Read the court documents report · Gulf News
impact_source: Read about the 36% share · Search Engine Land
deal_value: $20bn in 2022, and 36% of Safari search revenue, revealed in court
